## Overview of the Presentation

- Definition of high bile duct obstruction
- Indications for biliary drainage
- Endoscopic vs. percutaneous drainage
- Preprocedure preparation
- Intraprocedural issues
- Postprocedure care
- Summary

---

## Defining High Bile Duct Obstruction

- Historically defined as above the cystic duct insertion into the common hepatic duct (CHD)
- More accurate definition: obstruction involving the hepatic confluence and the 2–4 cm of CHD distal to it
- Anatomic variability of the cystic duct/CHD confluence makes the historical definition inaccurate

---

## Causes of Hilar Obstruction

- **Hilar cholangiocarcinoma** (most common)
- **Intraductal tumor**
- Other malignancies:
    - Colorectal cancer
    - Breast cancer
    - Pancreatic cancer

---

## Goals of Treatment

- Define goals before committing to any drainage procedure
- Most important question: **Resectability?**
- Multidisciplinary team discussion is ideal:
    - Hepatobiliary surgeons
    - Interventional radiologists
    - Oncologists
    - Gastroenterologists

---

## Indications for Palliative Biliary Drainage

- Intractable pruritus
- Cholangitis
- Need to restore liver function for chemotherapy (agents with biliary metabolism/excretion)
- Access for intraluminal brachytherapy
- Diversion for bile leak

---

## Indications for Biliary Drainage (Detailed)

- **Not indicated** for isolated hyperbilirubinemia or imaging findings of dilation alone
- **Indicated** for:
    - Pruritus
    - Cholangitis
    - Lowering bilirubin for chemotherapy
    - Postoperative bile leaks (after biliary-enteric bypass)
    - Local treatment delivery (brachytherapy, photodynamic therapy)

---

## Quality of Life and Preoperative Drainage

- Relief of jaundice does not definitively improve QOL (Robson et al. trial)
- Percutaneous drainage of high obstruction does not significantly improve QOL except in patients with pruritus
- Controversy remains regarding preoperative drainage
- Preoperative drainage of future remnant liver often performed for:
    - Major hepatectomy
    - Before portal vein embolization

---

## Preoperative Drainage: Methods

- Endoscopic methods preferred for low obstruction (lower complication rate)
- Percutaneous methods preferred for high obstruction (reduces risk of cholangitis in undrained segments)
- Patients with Bismuth type II and higher are at high risk for multiple drainage procedures

---

## FIGURE 52.1: High vs. Low Bile Duct Obstruction

- **High bile duct obstruction**: at or above the confluence
- **Low bile duct obstruction**: below the common hepatic duct
- Segmental anatomy highlighted

---

## Endoscopic vs. Percutaneous Drainage

- **Low obstruction**: typically treated endoscopically
- **High obstruction**: traditionally treated percutaneously
- Percutaneous success rate is higher and complication rate lower
- Endoscopic techniques are evolving, but high obstruction should still be approached percutaneously (with rare exception)

---

## Randomized Trial of Percutaneous vs. Endoscopic Drainage

- Trial stopped prematurely due to high mortality (11%) in percutaneous group
- 11% mortality is much higher than recent reports
- SIR mortality threshold (2010): 1.7%
- Raises questions about operator experience and expertise in the trial

---

## Drawbacks of Endoscopic Drainage for High Obstruction

- Lack of ability to reliably target a specific liver area for drainage
- Risk of enteric contamination of undrained parts of the biliary tree (retrograde contrast injection)
- Inadequate preoperative drainage is common (Wiggers et al., 2015):
    - 38% (108/288) of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma patients required additional percutaneous procedures after ERCP

---

## FIGURE 52.2: Inadequate Endoscopic Drainage

- Image showing endoscopic stenting of right and left liver
- Repeat imaging reveals incomplete drainage
- Highlights the challenge of endoscopic approaches for high obstruction

---

## Endoscopic Ultrasound-Guided Drainage

- Linear-array echoendoscope allows for:
    - Choledochoduodenostomy
    - Hepaticogastrostomy
- Hepaticogastrostomy considered when:
    - Left lateral segment drainage is needed
    - Anatomy is favorable
    - Percutaneous approach is difficult
    - Risk of contaminating right bile ducts is prohibitive

---

## FIGURE 52.3: Right Liver Drainage of No Clinical Benefit

- Cases where draining the right liver would not help:
    - Tumor replacement of the liver
    - Occlusion of the right portal vein
- Hepaticogastrostomy may be an alternative

---

## Success and Complication Rates of EUS-Guided Drainage

- Some authors report high technical success with few complications
- Others report high technical success but less favorable complication and stent patency rates
- Most operators are early on the learning curve
- In skilled hands, this procedure can be gratifying, with relief of pruritus and bilirubin lowering without a percutaneous catheter

---

## Papillary Intraductal Tumor

- Endoscopic drainage is rarely indicated
- Inevitable tumor ingrowth into metallic stent leads to early occlusion
- Intraductal tumor can arise from:
    - Papillary cholangiocarcinoma
    - Colorectal metastases
    - Gallbladder cancer
    - Hepatocellular carcinoma
- Often direct extension of parenchymal metastasis into the duct

---

## Management of Intraductal Tumor

- Often require permanent indwelling catheter drainage
- Multi-sidehole catheter allows bile to drain around the tumor
- May be stented when the intraductal tumor can be effectively excluded

---

## Preprocedure Preparation: Imaging

- Importance of excellent preprocedure imaging cannot be overemphasized
- Minimum: contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen
- Ultrasound: useful to establish dilated ducts, level of obstruction, portal vein patency, intraductal tumor
- But ultrasound is **not adequate** for drainage planning

---

## MRCP for Biliary Imaging

- Provides detailed 3D rendering of obstructed bile ducts
- Effective at:
    - Delineating intraductal abnormalities
    - Depicting isolated bile ducts
- Shortcomings:
    - Poor visualization of surgical clips, calcifications, bony landmarks
    - Suboptimal if patient cannot breath-hold

---

## FIGURE 52.5: MRCP Rendering

- Detailed 3D rendering of obstructed bile ducts
- Delineates intraductal abnormalities
- Depicts isolated bile ducts

---

## CT Imaging for Drainage Planning

- Multi-slice CT in PACS environment allows 3D rendering
- Identifies relevant landmarks for targeting
- Demonstrates structures to avoid (liver tumors, bowel)
- Identifies ancillary findings:
    - Ascites
    - Hepatic lobar atrophy
    - Portal vein occlusion/encasement

---

## Estimating Functional Parenchyma

- Functional parenchyma = liver not replaced by tumor, with intact portal venous supply and hepatic venous drainage
- If 75% of parenchyma is replaced by tumor, even complete biliary drainage may not normalize bilirubin
- Portal vein occlusion leads to atrophy of affected segments

---

## FIGURE 52.6A: Right Hepatic Atrophy

- Volume of right hemiliver is greatly diminished
- Severe attenuation of the right portal vein (arrows)

---

## FIGURE 52.6B: Left Hepatic Atrophy

- Small size of left hemiliver
- Crowding of dilated bile ducts secondary to portal vein occlusion
- Endoscopic stent (asterisk) previously placed, patient returned with jaundice and cholangitis

---

## Drainage of Atrophied Liver

- Drainage of atrophied liver does not improve function
- Often difficult to manipulate catheters through obstructed/atrophied portion
- Results in external drainage catheter with no clinical benefit
- Only risks complications and degrades QOL

---

## Isolation of Biliary Tree

- Central tumors frequently obstruct right and left biliary tree, isolating them
- Obstruction may extend to sectoral, segmental, or subsegmental level
- Draining even a segment may relieve pruritus
- For lowering bilirubin, aim to drain at least 75% of liver to normalize bilirubin
- More than one catheter or stent may be needed

---

## Cholangitis as an Indication for Drainage

- Rarely the primary indication except in patients with:
    - Prior biliary instrumentation
    - Contaminated biliary tree (biliary-enteric bypass, cross-ampullary stenting, sphincterotomy)
- Draining an isolated region may contaminate other isolated parts
- This can lead to chronic recurrent cholangitis
- Should be anticipated and avoided if possible

---

## Preprocedure Laboratory Studies

- Complete blood count
- Hepatic function panel
- Coagulation studies (PT, INR, PTT)
- Serum bilirubin: draw within 24 hours of drainage
    - Bilirubin is typically rising; may be higher the morning after the procedure
    - Values drawn 48 hours after drainage more accurately predict effectiveness

---

## Coagulation Abnormalities

- Lack of bile salts in intestine impairs vitamin K absorption
- May result in elevated PT, INR, PTT
- Corrected by:
    - Vitamin K administration
    - Fresh frozen plasma (depending on urgency)

---

## Antibiotic Prophylaxis

- Given to all patients undergoing biliary drainage
- History of instrumentation and fever are highly predictive of bactibilia
- Up to 5% of patients without these signs may have positive bile cultures
- Broad coverage: ticarcillin-clavulanate or ceftriaxone
- Choice should reflect common biliary organisms at the institution
- For contaminated biliary tree: piperacillin-tazobactam (Zosyn)

---

## Psychological Preparation

- Manage patient expectations thoroughly
- Discuss possible outcomes, especially for high obstruction
- Patients should understand:
    - Internal drainage may not be achieved
    - Two or more catheters/stents may be required
    - Pruritus often resolves, but bilirubin may not normalize
    - Bilirubin may even increase
- Mitigates surprise or anger if multiple procedures are needed

---

## FIGURE 52.7A: Tumor Causing Severe Narrowing

- Obstruction caused by tumor severely narrows biliary tree up to secondary confluence on right

---

## FIGURE 52.7B: Catheter Placement and Compromise

- After placement of multiple sidehole catheter, right posterior sector is well drained
- Catheter compromises near-complete obstruction of right anterior division duct and left hepatic duct

---

## Approach: Right-Sided

- **Advantages:**
    - Right liver is larger and more accessible
    - Avoids direct x-ray exposure to hands
    - Direct approach to hepatic hilus and common bile duct
    - Easier catheter and guidewire manipulations
    - Fewer structures between skin and right liver (safer, lower bleeding risk)
- **Disadvantages:**
    - Intercostal catheter discomfort
    - Leaking of ascites around gravity-dependent catheter
- Mitigated with primary stent placement

---

## Anatomic Variant: Posterior Right Duct Joins Left

- Occurs in 20% of patients
- May add a 180-degree turn to approach the hilum
- Can be advantageous: approach from posterior right duct drains right posterior sector and entire left liver when posterior duct joins the left

---

## Approach: Left-Sided

- **Indications:**
    - Tumor extends above biliary confluence, isolating right and left ducts
    - Tumor involves secondary confluence or higher
    - Right hepatic duct shorter; tumor more likely to isolate right anterior/posterior sectoral ducts
    - Left medial/lateral sectors continue to communicate
    - Single catheter/stent on left may drain more functional parenchyma
    - Ascites: less leakage around left anterior catheter

---

## Image Guidance

- Fluoroscopic guidance is most common
- Ultrasound for left-sided puncture; less often for right
- Careful review of high-quality CT:
    - Identify radiopaque landmarks
    - Target specific region or duct
    - Important when isolation is suspected
- Previously placed stents, surgical clips, etc., can aid targeting

---

## Sedation

- General anesthesia not necessary but helpful when available
- Especially useful when:
    - Bile ducts are not dilated or minimally dilated
    - Patient has sleep apnea (variable respirations make targeting difficult)
- NPO for 8 hours before procedure
- Hydration and functional venous access essential
- Risk of sepsis and hypotension requiring rapid volume expansion

---

## Technical Aids: Multidetector CT (MDCT)

- Most significant technical development in recent years
- Ability to scan liver in a single breath hold
- Facilitates identification of level of obstruction and isolation likelihood
- Enables 3D mental image of biliary tree
- Anticipates normal variants of bile duct anatomy
- PACS workstations allow cross-reference of axial images with scout image for easier targeting

---

- Axial image from PACS workstation used for targeting specific ducts

---

## FIGURE 52.8B: Scout Image

- Simulated frontal radiograph used for programming scan extent

---

## FIGURE 52.8C: Final Catheter Placement

- Final catheter resides within the planned segment of the liver

## Drainage Catheter vs. Primary Stent Placement

- Decision based on:
    - Indication for drainage
    - Evidence of infected bile
    - Presence of blood or tumor in biliary tree
    - Cholangiographic findings
- Goal: solve the clinical problem with as few catheters/stents as possible
- Bile should drain internally when intervention is complete

---

## Primary Stent Placement: Considerations

- Presumed sterile biliary tree: attempt to stent without placing drainage catheter into duodenum
- Preserving sphincter of Oddi may reduce cholangitis risk if stent occludes
- Patients with high obstruction without cholangitis: may be stented primarily at initial procedure
- **Contraindications:**
    - Significant blood clot within intrahepatic ducts (impairs drainage)
    - Cholangitis (catheter manipulation minimized; stent later)

---

## Bismuth-Corlette Classification

- Classification of hepatic confluence obstruction (1975)
- **Types I–IV**
- Predictions based on preprocedure imaging, but may need modification based on cholangiography

---

## FIGURE 52.9: Bismuth-Corlette Classification

- **Type I:** Tumor below confluence
- **Type II:** Tumor involves confluence
- **Type III:** Tumor extends into right or left hepatic duct
- **Type IV:** Tumor involves both right and left ducts to secondary confluence

---

## Bismuth Type I Obstruction

- Entire liver can be drained with one catheter or stent
- Right and left ducts communicate freely
- Primary stent placement is appropriate (barring contraindications)

---

## Bismuth Type II Obstruction

- Cannot be completely drained with one catheter
- May be possible to opacify ducts on both sides
- Some suggest better survival with bilateral drainage
- Options:
    1. T-shaped configuration: one stent ipsilateral to contralateral, second stent from ipsilateral to common bile duct
    2. Y-shaped configuration: puncture contralateral side, place side-by-side stents

---

## FIGURE 52.10A: Bismuth Type II Obstruction

- Patient with cholangiocarcinoma
- Near-complete isolation of right and left hepatic ducts

---

## FIGURE 52.10B: T-Shaped Configuration

- Side-by-side T-shaped configuration
- One stent from left hepatic duct (LHD) to right hepatic duct
- Second stent from LHD into common bile duct (CBD)
- Stent ends short of duodenum, preserving sphincter

---

## FIGURE 52.11A: Type II Obstruction After Whipple

- Patient with pancreatic cancer after Whipple procedure
- Recurrence at biliary-enteric anastomosis
- Type II obstruction

---

## FIGURE 52.11B: Y-Shaped Configuration

- Side-by-side Y-shaped configuration stents
- Both stents approachable percutaneously or endoscopically if occlusion occurs

---

## Stent Configuration: Y vs. T

- **Y-shaped:**
    - More anatomic
    - If occlusion occurs, both stents approachable percutaneously or endoscopically
    - Better patency in type IV obstruction
- **T-shaped:**
    - One stent from ipsilateral to contralateral side
    - Second stent from ipsilateral into CBD

---

## Bismuth Type III or IV Obstruction

- Contralateral biliary tree not opacified
- If draining for pruritus alone: primary stent placement
- If draining to lower bilirubin for chemotherapy: stent considered if >30% of liver will be drained
- If bilirubin fails to fall: second drainage procedure can be performed
- Creative solutions: multiple stents into isolated parts of the liver

---

## Rule of Thumb: 30% Liver Drainage

- Series of 149 patients at Memorial Sloan Kettering:
    - 29% of patients with <1/3 of liver drained attained bilirubin <2 mg/dL
    - 51% of patients with >1/3 of liver drained attained bilirubin <2 mg/dL (P = .06)
- Stent placement may be considered when >30% of the liver can be drained

---

## Stent Patency

- No difference in patency for proximal vs. distal obstruction
- Significant difference in patency when more than one stent is placed
- Lower complication rates when stents placed primarily
- Mean patency of multiple stents: almost 6 months

---

## FIGURE 52.12: Multiple Stents for Complex Drainage

- Stents placed from:
    - Right anterior hepatic duct to CBD
    - Left hepatic duct to CBD
    - Left hepatic duct to residual undrained posterior right duct
- A: Without contrast
- B: After injection of contrast

---

## Postprocedure Care: Monitoring

- Patients monitored carefully for first 24 hours
- Signs of bleeding or sepsis
- Peripheral bile duct puncture minimizes serious bleeding complications

---

## Hemobilia

- Blood may enter bile duct during catheter exchanges
- Usually clears within 24 hours
- New or recurrent hemobilia within first few days: catheter malposition
    - Reposition catheter, often upsize
- Significant arterial bleeding is rare

---

## FIGURE 52.13A: Proper Hepatic Angiogram

- Patient with hemobilia and bleeding around catheter 1 week after drainage
- Spasm of right hepatic artery branch adjacent to catheter at duct puncture site (arrows)

---

## FIGURE 52.13B: Coil Embolization

- Right hepatic angiogram after coil embolization of right hepatic artery branch (arrows)

---

## Late Bleeding (>1 Week)

- Sudden onset
- Hemobilia and bleeding around catheter entry site
- Suspect arterial injury
- Angiographic study indicated
- Pseudoaneurysm or extravasation may be seen
- Any abnormality of adjacent hepatic arterial branch: presumptive evidence of injury
- Selective coil embolization of the branch

---

## Sepsis After Drainage

- Despite antibiotic prophylaxis, sepsis may occur
- Manifests as rigors with normal or low temperature, hypotension, fever
- Management:
    - Continued antibiotics
    - Intravascular volume expansion
    - Pressor support if necessary
- Blood cultures and bile cultures should be obtained

---

## Bile Leak Around Catheter

- Most often due to catheter malposition (sideholes outside biliary tree)
- Management: reposition catheter
- Other causes:
    - Inadequate sideholes above obstruction
    - Catheter occlusion
- Capped internal-external catheters: distal sidehole occlusion
    - Open to gravity drainage initially, then exchange catheter

---

## Ascites Leak Around Catheter

- Ascitic fluid may be bile-colored (mistaken for bile)
- Difficult to manage
- Best treatment: establish internal drainage with stent placement
- If cannot be stented:
    - Upsize catheter to tamponade site
    - Frequent paracentesis or Tenckhoff catheter drainage
    - Stoma device around entry site (last resort)

---

## Duodenal Obstruction or Impaired Motility

- Patients may be relegated to obligate external drainage
- Internal drainage not possible
- Management of external drainage catheters

---

## Summary: Key Points

- Malignant high bile duct obstruction presents unique challenges
- Outcome depends on:
    - Condition of underlying hepatic parenchyma
    - Degree of biliary tree isolation
    - Technical skills of the operator
- High-quality imaging and understanding of functional biliary anatomy are essential

---

## Summary: Pruritus and Bilirubin

- Pruritus may be palliated by draining even one segment of the liver
- Lowering bilirubin to normal/near-normal: best achieved by draining at least 30% of the liver (assuming relatively normal parenchyma)

---

## Summary: Contamination and Stent Placement

- Contamination of undrained biliary tree parts can lead to ongoing/recurrent cholangitis
- Primary stent placement should be considered when ≥30% of the liver can be drained at the initial procedure

---

## Take-Home Messages

1. Define goals of treatment before any procedure
2. High obstruction: percutaneous approach preferred
3. Excellent preprocedure imaging is critical
4. Functional parenchyma and isolation degree guide planning
5. Primary stent placement should be considered when possible
6. Manage patient expectations realistically
7. Monitor for complications: bleeding, sepsis, bile leak, ascites

---
